Germany.summary:
Germany's microelectronics sector, which accounts for 30% of Europe's wafer production capacity and contributes 4% directly and 15% indirectly to Germany's GDP, is crucial for the nation's industrial competitiveness and technological sovereignty. The European Chips Act and two IPCEIs have facilitated projects like the establishment of ESMC, the expansion of Infineon's chip factory, and the creation of the APECS Pilot Line at Research Fab Microelectronics Germany (FMD).

Future efforts, supported by EU funding until 2027, will focus on developing existing economic and technological strengths, advancing new microelectronics technologies through existing Pilot Lines and research, and strengthening supply chain resilience. The Federal Government's strategy prioritizes research in "Chip Design Capabilities" and "Lab to Fab" technology transfer focusing on advanced packaging, supporting the microelectronics talent pipeline, and incentivizing innovative microelectronics production in Germany, including semiconductor production and advanced packaging.

Germany.title: German data centre landscape –
Germany.summary:
Germany is Europe's largest data center hub, with over 2,000 data centers and an installed IT power demand of over 2,700 MW as of March 2025. Capacity has more than doubled since 2010, reaching 2,730 MW in 2024, and is forecast to grow to 4,800 MW by 2030. The Frankfurt-Rhine/Main metropolitan area remains the primary concentration, with Berlin/Brandenburg and Cologne/Düsseldorf emerging as new hubs.

Data centers and smaller IT installations in Germany consumed 20 TWh of electricity in 2024, representing 4% of Germany's gross electricity consumption. This is projected to rise to 31 TWh by 2030 and nearly 80 TWh by 2045, comprising 6% of projected gross electricity consumption. Germany has set a PUE value of 1.2 as a legal requirement for new data centers from July 2026, while China has a PUE requirement of 1.3 in temperate regions and 1.25 in cooler regions from 2025.

Germany.title: GreenTech Innovation
Germany.summary:
Germany's Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action (BMWK) published details on February 24, 2025, regarding its "GreenTech Innovation Competition" technology program. This initiative aims to leverage digitalization for Germany's green transition, supporting the country's climate and environmental protection targets and strengthening its role in digital technologies. The program focuses on using digital technologies like AI, digital twins, and edge/cloud computing to reduce emissions and resource consumption, while also improving the sustainability of digital technologies themselves.

The publication highlights 21 specific projects, including ARKIDES, which runs from May 2023 to April 2026. ARKIDES, coordinated by Jürgen Mangelberger, focuses on automated recycling and disassembly of electronics using AI, aiming to increase re-utilization rates for materials and components from large electrical devices. Another project, BeverGreen, coordinated by Jochen Wiecha and also running from May 2023 to April 2026, is developing an assistance system based on use-specific ontologies.

France.title: Economic Stakes and Role for France?
France.summary:
France lacks major companies in global chip manufacturing and computing power rental markets, with US companies like Nvidia (85% GPU market share in 2023) and hyperscalers such as Amazon (46% of France's cloud computing market in 2021), Microsoft (17%), and Alphabet (8%) dominating. However, France benefits from a skilled workforce, ranking fourth in 2022 for the origin of elite AI researchers and fifth for where they work. French AI research also ranked fourth in Europe for scientific publications in 2021.

Despite a thriving research ecosystem with institutions like CNRS and INRIA, France struggles to retain talent due to lower pay and career opportunities compared to foreign institutions. Private investment in AI funding rounds in France totaled €7.2 billion from 2013-2023, significantly less than the US (€289 billion) and China (€89.3 billion). French and European initiatives like Tibi and InvestEU aim to increase funding for late-stage tech firms, as 82% of European scale-up funding rounds between 2013 and 2023 involved a foreign lead investor.

This market dominance by a few large firms raises concerns about economic efficiency, fair competition, and national sovereignty.

France.title: Foreign Investment Screening in France
France.summary:
In 2023, France received 309 applications for foreign investment screening, a slight decrease from 325 in 2022. The French Treasury authorized 135 transactions, with 60 (44%) of these authorizations being conditional. Of the authorized investments, 21.5% were in inherently sensitive activities, 63.7% in essential infrastructure, goods, or services, and 14.8% were mixed. 67.3% of ultimate investors were from non-EU/EEA countries, primarily the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada, while 32.7% were from EU/EEA countries, mainly Germany, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands.

As of January 1, 2024, new measures have been implemented to strengthen foreign investment screening. The threshold for screening listed French companies for non-European investors has been permanently lowered to a 10% voting rights stake. Screening now also applies to branches of foreign legal entities in France, and to activities related to the extraction, processing, and recycling of critical raw materials, as well as R&D in all low-carbon technologies and photonics. A new electronic platform, "Plateforme IEF," was established on October 1, 2023, to streamline the application process.

On April 13, 2023, France and the Netherlands signed a Pact for Innovation and Sustainable Growth, aiming to boost public-private partnerships. French Ministers Roland Lescure (Industry), Micky Adriaansens (Economy and Climate), and Liesje Schreinemacher (Foreign Trade), along with representatives from MEDEF and VNO-NCW, signed the pact. This agreement builds on the August 2021 France-Netherlands Declaration and March 2022 intergovernmental consultations.

The pact focuses on strengthening cooperation in key economic fields such as semiconductors, quantum technologies, photonics, sustainable industry (including decarbonization, renewable and low-carbon energies, nuclear, hydrogen, critical and biobased raw materials, circular economy, and decarbonized energy storage), agriculture, agri-food, and sustainable mobility. A steering committee will be established for implementation. Additionally, France and the Netherlands will organize a seminar and mission from Grenoble to Brainport Eindhoven in the second half of 2023 to facilitate exchanges in the chips sector, and CEA (FR) and TNO (NL) signed a Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen strategic cooperation in energy.

France.title: No. 257  March 2020 The Impact of Oil Prices on the US Economy
France.summary:
Since the late 2000s, US oil production doubled from 5 million barrels per day (Mb/d) in 2008 to 11 Mb/d in 2018, largely due to unconventional drilling techniques like hydraulic fracturing. Natural gas production also increased from 12 Mb/d oil equivalent (Mboe/d) in 2008 to 17 Mboe/d in 2018. This growth reduced US oil energy dependence from 57% in 2008 to 11% in 2018 and improved the oil trade balance from –$386bn in 2008 to –$50bn in 2018. The US accounted for 13% of global oil production in 2018, up from 7% in 2008, and 21.5% of global natural gas production in 2015.

The breakeven price for American shale oil decreased from over $80 per barrel in 2010 to nearly $40 per barrel in early 2017. While historically negative, the impact of oil price increases on US GDP has become less clear-cut since 2010. Increases now positively affect investment in the hydrocarbon sector, countering negative effects on consumption. Estimated elasticities of US GDP to oil prices after less than a year now range between –0.124 and +0.017.

European Commission.title: digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu
European Commission.summary:
The European Chips Act, which entered into force on September 21, 2023, aims to double Europe's global market share of semiconductors to 20% by 2030. The EU currently holds approximately 10% of the global market share and is heavily reliant on third-country suppliers, with nearly 80% headquartered outside the EU. The Act targets a leading role in designing and manufacturing microchips down to 2 nanometers nodes and below, with 3 nanometer chips entering production in Taiwan in 2022 and 2 nanometer chips expected in 2024.

The Chips Act is structured around three pillars: the "Chips for Europe initiative" for design tools, pilot lines, and equity finance via the Chips Fund; "Security of supply and resilience" through investor-friendly frameworks for Integrated Production Facilities (IPF) and Open EU Foundries (OEF); and "Monitoring and crisis response" via tools like Supply Chain Alert Notification (SCAN) and the European Semiconductor Board (ESB). The Act is expected to generate over €43 billion in public investments, contributing to a total of more than €100 billion in policy-driven investment by 2030, including public and private funds. Key achievements include the inauguration of Chips JU and launch of €1.67 billion in funding for 4 pilot lines on November 30, 2023, and the approval of a €2 billion Italian State aid measure for STMicroelectronics on May 31, 2024.

QinetiQ has developed a low-cost thermal imaging sensor for military dismounted operations, utilizing Foundry Uncooled Thermal Imaging (FUNTI) technology. This technology manufactures infrared detector arrays on a standard CMOS production process, significantly reducing costs compared to traditional thermal imaging detectors which typically cost thousands of dollars. The resulting sensors, while having modest performance with a short range of up to 100 meters, are designed to be disposable and deployed in large numbers to monitor extensive terrain, eliminate dead ground, and operate effectively in complex environments like urban settings.

It achieves a Noise Equivalent Temperature Difference (NETD) of 0.3K to 0.35K at f/1, and employs an over-sampling technique with a state-of-the-art Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) to achieve a high dynamic range approaching 20 bits.

Chatham House.title: CONTROLLING THE INTERNATIONAL TRADE IN ILLEGALLY LOGGED TIMBER AND WOOD PRODUCTS
Chatham House.summary:
A February 2002 study by Duncan Brack, Kevin Gray, and Gavin Hayman for the UK Department for International Development examines methods for importing/consuming governments to deny market access to illegally logged timber and wood products. The report stresses that establishing a system to identify legally produced logs and wood products is technically feasible, requiring sufficient resources and political will. Key recommendations include using technologically sophisticated solutions instead of simple paper-based certificates, implementing comprehensive chain-of-custody monitoring with independent third-party auditing, providing capacity-building support for system setup and enforcement, and systematically collecting and exchanging export/import data, potentially with a central monitoring function similar to WCMC for CITES.

To close markets to illegal products, consumer countries can make their sale or import illegal through new legislation. This legislation could either adopt a definition of illegality based on producer country laws (like the US Lacey Act) or establish internationally agreed standards, such as evidence of independently verified chain-of-custody monitoring. A step-wise implementation of measures is suggested, including encouraging voluntary industry action to source only legal products, establishing favorable tariff preferences, implementing effective government procurement policies, and enacting Lacey Act-type legislation. The report also suggests legislation outlawing the import and sale of products not positively identified as legal, with time for publicizing impacts, providing capacity-building, establishing robust identification systems, and negotiating bilateral/regional agreements.

all_summaries.title: Foreign Investment Screening in France

all_summaries.summary:

Natural gas production also increased from 12 Mb/d oil equivalent (Mboe/d) in 2008 to 17 Mboe/d in 2018. This growth reduced US oil energy dependence from 57% in 2008 to 11% in 2018 and improved the oil trade balance from –$386bn in 2008 to –$50bn in 2018. The US accounted for 13% of global oil production in 2018, up from 7% in 2008, and 21.5% of global natural gas production in 2015.

The breakeven price for American shale oil decreased from over $80 per barrel in 2010 to nearly $40 per barrel in early 2017. While historically negative, the impact of oil price increases on US GDP has become less clear-cut since 2010. Increases now positively affect investment in the hydrocarbon sector, countering negative effects on consumption. Estimated elasticities of US GDP to oil prices after less than a year now range between –0.124 and +0.017.

The Act is expected to generate over €43 billion in public investments, contributing to a total of more than €100 billion in policy-driven investment by 2030, including public and private funds. Key achievements include the inauguration of Chips JU and launch of €1.67 billion in funding for 4 pilot lines on November 30, 2023, and the approval of a €2 billion Italian State aid measure for STMicroelectronics on May 31, 2024.

all_summaries.summary:
QinetiQ has developed a low-cost thermal imaging sensor for military dismounted operations, utilizing Foundry Uncooled Thermal Imaging (FUNTI) technology. This technology manufactures infrared detector arrays on a standard CMOS production process, significantly reducing costs compared to traditional thermal imaging detectors which typically cost thousands of dollars. The resulting sensors, while having modest performance with a short range of up to 100 meters, are designed to be disposable and deployed in large numbers to monitor extensive terrain, eliminate dead ground, and operate effectively in complex environments like urban settings.

The sensor design incorporates a 64x64 pixel array with a 75-micron pitch, yielding a nominal detector resistance of 2.3 kΩ at room temperature. It achieves a Noise Equivalent Temperature Difference (NETD) of 0.3K to 0.35K at f/1, and employs an over-sampling technique with a state-of-the-art Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) to achieve a high dynamic range approaching 20 bits.

all_summaries.title: CONTROLLING THE INTERNATIONAL TRADE IN ILLEGALLY LOGGED TIMBER AND WOOD PRODUCTS
all_summaries.summary:
A February 2002 study by Duncan Brack, Kevin Gray, and Gavin Hayman for the UK Department for International Development examines methods for importing/consuming governments to deny market access to illegally logged timber and wood products. The report stresses that establishing a system to identify legally produced logs and wood products is technically feasible, requiring sufficient resources and political will. Key recommendations include using technologically sophisticated solutions instead of simple paper-based certificates, implementing comprehensive chain-of-custody monitoring with independent third-party auditing, providing capacity-building support for system setup and enforcement, and systematically collecting and exchanging export/import data, potentially with a central monitoring function similar to WCMC for CITES.

To close markets to illegal products, consumer countries can make their sale or import illegal through new legislation. This legislation could either adopt a definition of illegality based on producer country laws (like the US Lacey Act) or establish internationally agreed standards, such as evidence of independently verified chain-of-custody monitoring. A step-wise implementation of measures is suggested, including encouraging voluntary industry action to source only legal products, establishing favorable tariff preferences, implementing effective government procurement policies, and enacting Lacey Act-type legislation. The report also suggests legislation outlawing the import and sale of products not positively identified as legal, with time for publicizing impacts, providing capacity-building, establishing robust identification systems, and negotiating bilateral/regional agreements.
